question: Which statement best describes Behavior vs implementation?
options: @testing-library/user-event simulates the full sequence a real interaction triggers (focus, keydown, input, keyup) instead of a single raw DOM event like fireEvent. It is the recommended way to model clicks and typing, and its modern API is asynchronous — you must await each call so the resulting state updates and re-renders flush before you assert.

RTL's recommended query priority is accessibility-first: getByRole (with an accessible name), then getByLabelText/getByText, then getByDisplayValue/getByAltText, with getByTestId only as a last resort. Role queries hit the accessibility tree, so a passing test doubles as an a11y check and resembles how real users and assistive tech locate elements. Leaning on data-testid decouples tests from real usage.

The three query families differ in what they do when an element is missing, and choosing the right one makes intent and failure messages clear. getBy throws if absent (assert present now), queryBy returns null (assert absence), and findBy returns a promise that retries until the element appears (assert async appearance). The *AllBy variants return arrays for multiple matches.

The core RTL philosophy is to assert on what a user observes — rendered text, accessible roles, interaction results — never on internal state, prop values, method names, or CSS classes. Implementation-detail tests break on harmless refactors and can pass while the UI is actually broken, giving false confidence. RTL deliberately exposes no API to read internals so you are guided toward durable behavior tests.

question: Which statement best describes Queries (getBy / queryBy / findBy)?
options: The three query families differ in what they do when an element is missing, and choosing the right one makes intent and failure messages clear. getBy throws if absent (assert present now), queryBy returns null (assert absence), and findBy returns a promise that retries until the element appears (assert async appearance). The *AllBy variants return arrays for multiple matches.

When UI updates after a promise (e.g. a fetch), use findBy* to wait for a single element to appear, or waitFor for any assertion that must eventually pass (something removed, a mock called). Both are wrapped in act and retry until they pass or time out — so you never reach for arbitrary setTimeout/sleep, which is the main cause of flaky tests.

Custom hooks can't be called outside a component, so renderHook (from @testing-library/react) mounts them in a test harness and exposes result.current. You assert on the returned values across re-renders, and use act/waitFor for async transitions like loading to loaded. This isolates hook logic without coupling to any particular consuming component.

RTL tests run in jsdom inside Node, not a real browser — fast enough for the inner loop and CI on every commit. jsdom implements enough of the DOM and accessibility tree for role/text queries, but it does not lay out or paint pixels. Visual, layout, and true cross-browser concerns belong in real-browser tools like Playwright or Cypress, reserved for a few critical flows.
